title: new and delete
learningGoals: make a variable on the heap with new

youtube.title: C++ new and delete: The Heap Explained | C++ Programming EP 46
youtube.description: In this episode you will make a variable on the heap with new, free it with delete and explain stack and heap, with Xecxec the crab. 0:00 Intro · 0:15 new and delete · 0:58 One box on the heap · 1:38 Stack and heap · 2:08 Second program · 3:08 Recap · 3:38 Bug of the Day · 4:26 Challenge · 4:46 Next episode

thumbnail.visual: big text "NEW + DELETE" in tomato on lilac; Xecxec next to a crab borrowing a box from a warehouse and returning it; thin black border and drop shadow.
thumbnail.pose: Xecxec next to a crab borrowing a box from a warehouse and returning it

scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: Today we ask for memory ourselves. We borrow a box from the heap, and we give it back when we finish.

scenes.onScreen: "new and delete": numbered lines (1. New asks the heap for a box; 2. Delete gives the box back; 3. Every new needs one delete) and an analogy card: a library book: you borrow it with new, and you must return it with delete
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: Local variables live on the stack. They appear and disappear by themselves. The heap is a big pool of memory that you manage yourself. New asks the heap for a box, and gives you its address. Delete returns the box. If you forget, the box is lost until the program ends. That is a memory leak. Think of a library book. You borrow it with new, and you must return it with delete.
points: New asks the heap for a box

analogy.title: new and delete
analogy.body: A library book: you borrow it with new, and you must return it with delete

scenes.onScreen: heap.cpp: new makes an int on the heap, delete frees it
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right
scenes.narration: [HL 5] New makes an int on the heap and sets it to five. It returns the address, and p stores it. [HL 6] Star p reads five. [HL 7] We change the value to six. [HL 9] Delete gives the box back to the heap. After delete, p still holds the old address, so do not use p again.

scenes.onScreen: p lives on the stack, and the int lives on the heap
scenes.animation: Boxes pop in one by one with size and address tags; arrows draw on as the narrator mentions them; regions are labelled; pop per box
scenes.narration: Look at the two regions. P is a normal local variable on the stack. It dies at the end of the function. The int lives on the heap. It stays until you delete it. If you lose p before you delete, nobody can ever free that box.

scenes.onScreen: heaparray.cpp: new with square brackets makes an array
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 5] New with square brackets makes an array of three ints on the heap. [HL 6] The loop multiplies each item by ten. [HL 9] The output is ten, twenty, thirty. [HL 10] An array made with new square brackets needs delete square brackets. A plain delete is a bug.

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the compile command types with key-tick, the run command types, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as heaparray dot cpp. Compile it with g plus plus. Then run the program. The program prints ten, twenty and thirty.

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One. The stack holds local variables, and the heap holds boxes you manage. Two. New asks the heap for a box. Three. Delete gives the box back. Four. Use delete with square brackets for an array. Pause the video. Say these ideas out loud, one time, slowly.
points: The stack holds local variables, and the heap holds boxes you manage.
New asks the heap for a box.
Use delete with square brackets for an array.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: The wrong delete
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; the g++ warning appears in tomato; the fix slides in and the warning goes away with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. We make an array with new square brackets, but we free it with plain delete. The compiler warns about a mismatched allocation function. The two forms must match. New square brackets pairs with delete square brackets.

scenes.onScreen: I borrowed a box from the heap and forgot to return it. Now I have a leak in my budget.
scenes.animation: Full tomato screen, card flips in with a rimshot, Xecxec snaps his claw
scenes.narration: I borrowed a box from the heap and forgot to return it. Now I have a leak in my budget.

scenes.onScreen: Task card: make and free a heap array
scenes.animation: Task card pops in; checklist ticks with a pop; Xecxec holds a tiny pen
scenes.narration: Your challenge: Make an array of four ints on the heap. Fill it with the squares one, four, nine and sixteen. Print it, and free it. Write your answer in the comments.

scenes.animation: Next-episode card slides up with a whoosh; right side stays empty for end-screen elements; sign-off text types in
scenes.narration: Next time: dynamic arrays. Keep coding, says Xecxec!

bug.error:
Compiler output (a warning, the program still builds):

heaparray.cpp: In function 'int main()':
heaparray.cpp:7:12: warning: 'void operator delete(void*, std::size_t)' called on pointer returned from a mismatched allocation function [-Wmismatched-new-delete]
    7 |     delete a;
      |            ^
heaparray.cpp:5:32: note: returned from 'void* operator new [](std::size_t)'
    5 |     int* a = new int[3]{1, 2, 3};
bug.why: New with square brackets must pair with delete with square brackets. A plain delete frees the memory in the wrong way, and the result is undefined.

pun: "I borrowed a box from the heap and forgot to return it. Now I have a leak in my budget."
challenge: Make an array of four ints on the heap. Fill it with the squares one, four, nine and sixteen. Print it, and free it.
challengeAnswer: Use new int with four in square brackets. Fill with i plus one squared. Print the items, then call delete with square brackets.
